newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey c.bank acts to meet pre-holiday cash demand.
newsitem.headline: Turkey c.bank acts to meet pre-holiday cash demand.

text.p: Turkey's central bank bought $400 million for lira and lent 160 trillion lira to banks in the past week to meet increased cash demand ahead of a long holiday, its governor Gazi Ercel said on Thursday.
"We bought $400 million for 50 trillion lira and injected another 160 trillion lira through open market and interbank operations," Ercel told Reuters.
"As a result of foreign currency purchases, our foreign exchange reserve rose to $16.1 billion," he added.
After the central bank operations, banknotes in circulation rose to a record high of 686.1 trillion lira on Wednesday.

It has risen about 50 percent since April 9 when the monetary expansion started after the treasury auctioned 133 trillion lira of two year bonds against its redemption of 200 trillion lira and left 67 trillion lira idle in the market.
"Most of this (recently injected) money will return by the end of this month after the holiday. Then monetary aggregates will return to their normal levels," Ercel said.
Cash demand always increases ahead of religous holidays in Turkey. Mid-month public sector salary and pension payments of 216 trillion lira this week aggravated cash demand.
Turkish capital and money markets will close at mid-day on Thursday for the Islamic holiday of Eid al-Adha and Children's Day national holiday. They will reopen on April 24.
Thousands of retired state employees lined up in front of bank branches this week and some branches failed to pay salaries due to insufficient cash positions.
Two people have died of heart attacks while wating in the salary queues.

Deputy Prime Minister Tansu Ciller said state bank Ziraat Bankasi would continue to pay salaries. "We may keep Ziraat Bankasi branches open on the first day of holiday for payments if needed," she said.
Opposition party members described the payment problem as a "scandal" and called for the government's resignation.

Bankers say the volume of banknotes in circulation is expected to shrink gradually after the holiday. However they fear that the sharp monetary expansion would fuel April inflation to be announced on May 4.
Some bankers say the central bank may increase interest rates later this month to accelerate the return of excess liquidity which may otherwise shift towards foreign currency.
Central Bank governor Ercel also declined press reports that the bank met cash demand by printing fresh banknotes.
"We used our buffer stocks which all the central banks hold," he said.
